questions.questionText: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in an array?
questions.hint: Arrays store elements contiguously in memory.
questions.explanation: Arrays provide O(1) constant-time access by index because elements are stored at contiguous memory addresses.

questions.questionText: Which data structure follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle?
questions.hint: Think of a stack of plates.
questions.explanation: A Stack follows LIFO: the last element pushed is the first to be popped.

questions.questionText: What is the main advantage of a LinkedList over an ArrayList?
options: Faster insertion and deletion at any position
questions.hint: No shifting of elements is needed.
questions.explanation: LinkedList provides O(1) insertion/deletion at known positions (no element shifting), while ArrayList requires O(n) shifting.

questions.questionText: What is a binary search tree (BST)?
options: A tree where each node has exactly two children
A tree where left child < parent < right child
A tree with only leaf nodes
A balanced tree with equal depths
questions.hint: The ordering property is the key characteristic.
questions.explanation: A BST is a binary tree where for every node, all values in the left subtree are less than the node, and all values in the right subtree are greater.

questions.questionText: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching in an unbalanced BST?
questions.hint: An unbalanced BST can degenerate into a linked list.
questions.explanation: In the worst case (e.g., inserting sorted data), a BST becomes a linked list with O(n) search time. Balanced BSTs (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee O(log n).

questions.questionText: Which data structure uses key-value pairs for storage?
questions.hint: You look up values using their associated keys.
questions.explanation: A Hash Table (Map) stores data as key-value pairs, allowing O(1) average-case lookup by key.

options: When two keys have the same value
When two different keys produce the same hash code
When the hash table is full
questions.hint: The hash function maps different inputs to the same bucket.
questions.explanation: A hash collision occurs when two different keys produce the same hash code, mapping to the same bucket. Resolved via chaining (linked lists) or open addressing.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between a singly linked list and a doubly linked list?
options: Doubly linked lists have references to both next and previous nodes
Singly linked lists use more memory
questions.hint: One can traverse in both directions.
questions.explanation: A singly linked list has nodes with only a 'next' pointer. A doubly linked list has both 'next' and 'prev' pointers, enabling bidirectional traversal.

questions.questionText: What is the space complexity of a recursive algorithm that makes n recursive calls?
options: O(n) due to the call stack
questions.hint: Each recursive call adds a frame to the call stack.
questions.explanation: Each recursive call uses stack space for its frame (local variables, return address). With n recursive calls, the space complexity is O(n).

questions.questionText: Which sorting algorithm has the best average-case time complexity?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort has O(n log n) average and worst-case time complexity, making it the most consistently efficient among common comparison-based sorts.

options: A queue that processes elements alphabetically
A queue where elements are dequeued based on priority, not insertion order
A faster version of a regular queue
A queue limited to a fixed size
questions.hint: The element with the highest priority is served first.
questions.explanation: A priority queue orders elements by priority (typically using a heap). The highest-priority element is always dequeued first, regardless of insertion order.

questions.questionText: What is the time complexity of inserting into a heap?
questions.hint: The element may need to 'bubble up' through the tree levels.
questions.explanation: Inserting into a heap takes O(log n) because the new element is added at the bottom and then 'sifted up' through at most log n levels to maintain the heap property.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Deque interface in Java?
options: To create a double-ended queue that supports insertion and removal at both ends
To delete elements from a queue
questions.explanation: Deque (Double-Ended Queue) allows insertion and removal at both the front and rear. It can be used as both a stack (LIFO) and a queue (FIFO).

questions.questionText: What is the time complexity of linear search?
questions.hint: It checks each element one by one.
questions.explanation: Linear search examines each element sequentially until a match is found or the end is reached, giving O(n) worst-case time complexity.

questions.questionText: What is the time complexity of binary search?
questions.hint: It halves the search space at each step.
questions.explanation: Binary search works on sorted arrays by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half, achieving O(log n) time complexity.
